decks.name: MDF & pot odds
decks.description: The defence maths behind the MDF Range Tool.

cards.title: Minimum Defense Frequency
cards.body: MDF = pot / (pot + bet). Defend at least that share of your range or villain profits by betting any two cards. The flip side is your fold cap: fold % = bet / (pot + bet).

cards.title: Pot odds
cards.body: Break-even equity to call = bet / (pot + bet). A half-pot bet lays 3:1, so you need 25%. Same formula as the fold half of MDF — MDF is that number applied to your whole range instead of one hand.

cards.title: Rule of 2 and 4
cards.body: On the flop with two cards to come, outs x 4 approximates your equity. On the turn with one card to come, outs x 2. Shade the flop number down when you hold 9+ outs, since it overstates by a few points.

cards.question: Pot is 100. Villain bets 50. What share of your range should you continue with?
Villain bets 75 into 100. What equity do you need for the call to break even?
You hold a flush draw on the flop (9 outs). Roughly what is your equity by the river?
cards.explanation: 9 outs x 4 = 36%. The true number is about 35%, so the rule barely overstates here.

decks.name: Preflop heuristics
decks.description: Opening, defending and 3-betting shortcuts for MTT play.

cards.title: Rule of 5-6-7 (BB defence)
cards.body: Defending the big blind vs a late-position open at ~40bb: call every suited hand, and take offsuit hands down to the 5x, 6x or 7x bar depending on how late the opener sat. Later position, lower bar.

cards.title: Position widens everything
cards.body: Every step closer to the button widens your opening range roughly 1.5x. UTG opens ~15%, hijack ~20%, cutoff ~27%, button ~45%, small blind ~40% with a 3-bet-or-fold lean.

cards.title: 3-bet or fold under 25bb
cards.body: Below about 25bb, flatting out of position leaves an unplayable stack-to-pot ratio postflop. Turn marginal flats into 3-bet shoves or folds, and keep flats for position and deep stacks.

cards.back: About 15% — 77+, ATs+, KJs+, QJs, JTs, AQo+
About 45% — all pairs, all suited aces and kings, most suited connectors, offsuit broadways down to A2o/K9o

cards.question: Which hand class does the big blind defend most often vs a button open?
cards.explanation: Suited hands realise the most equity from out of position, so BB defence keeps every suited combo before it reaches for offsuit hands.

cards.question: You open the cutoff and the button 3-bets. Roughly what portion of your opening range should continue?
cards.explanation: Against a typical 3-bet size you defend around 40% of the range you opened, mixing 4-bets with calls and folding the weakest opens outright.

decks.name: Tournament spots
decks.description: ICM, stack depth and bounty rules of thumb.

cards.title: SPR sets your commitment
cards.body: Stack-to-pot ratio below 3 means top pair is usually committing. Between 3 and 6 you want two pair or better to stack off. Above 6 you need a strong draw or a big made hand.

cards.title: ICM tightens calls, not shoves
cards.body: Near a pay jump, calling ranges tighten hard because busting costs real money, while shoving ranges stay wide because fold equity is worth more. Shove wide, call tight.

cards.title: Bounties widen calls
cards.body: In a PKO, a bounty you can win outright is worth extra equity in the pot. Covering a short stack lets you call several percentage points wider than the chip maths alone would allow.

cards.front: SPR after a single raise and one caller preflop
cards.back: Usually 4 to 6 — the two-pair-or-better zone for stacking off

cards.question: On the money bubble with a big stack, how should you adjust vs the short stacks?
options: Open tighter and avoid all confrontation
Open wider and attack their blinds
Call their shoves wider than usual
Play the same as any other stage
cards.answer: Open wider and attack their blinds
cards.explanation: Short stacks cannot call without risking elimination at a pay jump, so a big stack profits by applying pressure — while still calling their shoves tightly.

decks.name: Combo maths
decks.description: Counting combos, and why the 13x13 grid misleads you about them.

cards.body: A pair has 6 combos, a suited hand 4, an offsuit hand 12. Every combo count you will ever need preflop comes from those three numbers.

cards.title: The grid lies about frequency
cards.body: Suited and offsuit each take 78 of the 169 cells — the same 46% of the grid. But offsuit is three times the combos, so it is 70.6% of the hands you are actually dealt against 23.5% suited. Equal area on screen, very unequal at the table.

cards.title: Offsuit widens a range three times faster
cards.body: Dropping your offsuit floor one rank adds 12 combos per hand; dropping the suited floor adds 4. Axs+ is 48 combos, Axo+ is 144 — same twelve cells, triple the weight. Watch the offsuit bars when you are tuning an opening range.

cards.title: Blockers cut combos, not hands
cards.body: Holding one ace leaves villain 3 aces, so AA drops from 6 combos to C(3,2) = 3 — halved. Holding an ace and a king cuts AK from 16 to 9. Card removal bites hardest on the exact hands you are worried about.

cards.front: Combos in AK, suited and offsuit together
Share of a full range that is pairs
Share of a full range that is suited
Share of a full range that is offsuit
How much more often is an offsuit hand dealt than its suited twin?

cards.question: How many hand combinations are there in a full range?
cards.explanation: C(52,2) = 52 x 51 / 2 = 1,326. 169 is the number of hand types, not combos. 2,652 is 52 x 51, which counts each hand twice.

cards.question: What share of a full range is pocket pairs?
cards.explanation: 13 pairs x 6 combos = 78, and 78 / 1,326 = 5.9%. The 7.7% trap is the share of grid cells (13 of 169), which is not the same thing.

cards.question: What share of a full range is suited hands?
cards.explanation: 78 suited types x 4 combos = 312, and 312 / 1,326 = 23.5%. The 46.2% trap is the share of grid cells — suited fills 78 of 169 squares but only a quarter of the combos.

cards.question: What share of a full range is offsuit hands?
cards.explanation: 78 offsuit types x 12 combos = 936, and 936 / 1,326 = 70.6%. Offsuit takes the same 46.2% of grid cells as suited, but three times the combos.

cards.question: You hold A♠K♦. How many combos of AA can villain still have?
cards.explanation: Three aces remain, and C(3,2) = 3. Holding a single ace halves villain aces from 6 combos to 3.

cards.question: You hold A♠A♥. How many combos of AK can villain have?
cards.explanation: Two aces are left and all four kings, so 2 x 4 = 8 — half the usual 16.

cards.question: Villain shows up with exactly JJ+ and AK. How many combos is that?
cards.explanation: JJ, QQ, KK, AA is 4 x 6 = 24, and AK is 16 (4 suited + 12 offsuit). 24 + 16 = 40.

cards.question: Which adds more combos to an opening range: every suited ace, or every offsuit ace?
cards.explanation: Both are twelve cells on the grid, but Axs+ is 48 combos and Axo+ is 144. Offsuit hands carry 12 combos each against 4.

cards.question: A range of every pocket pair and nothing else is what percentage of hands?
cards.explanation: 78 combos of 1,326. All thirteen pairs together are still a very narrow range.

cards.question: You are dealt a hand at random. Which is most likely?
cards.explanation: 12 combos beats 6 for a pair and 4 for a suited hand. This is why a drill has to deal combo-weighted — picking a random grid square would show you suited hands about three times too often.

cards.question: How many suited hand types are there in the grid?
cards.explanation: C(13,2) = 78 ways to pick two different ranks. There are the same 78 offsuit types, plus 13 pairs, giving 169 cells. 312 is the suited combo count, not the type count.

cards.question: Your range is 22+ only. Roughly how many combos have you got?
cards.explanation: 13 pairs x 6 = 78 combos, which is 5.9% of all hands.
